source: Cook, Goodman & Schulz (2011) Where science starts, full text re-read, Experiment 1
finding: Full text confirms the earlier cell counts. Children who saw ambiguous bead evidence pulled the pair apart and tested each bead; children who saw unambiguous evidence mostly did not.
numbers: Exp 1: 60 preschoolers, 20 per condition (3 conditions). Informative experiment: All Beads 1/20 (5%); Some Beads B 9/20 (45%); Some Beads AB 10/20 (50%). 65% of All Beads children never pulled the pair apart. All Beads vs Some Beads B chi2(1,N=40)=8.53, p<.005; vs AB chi2=10.16, p<.005. B vs AB chi2=0.10, ns. Coder agreement 95% (kappa .90). Play variety did not differ across conditions.
limits: Small cells. Six children excluded for experimental error. No computed EIG per child; fit is qualitative.
agent_relevance: Closes the 'only abstract re-read' worry in the critique: cell counts now rest on the full paper.

source: Cook et al. (2011) Experiment 2 (design your own test), full text
finding: When children had to invent the test (stuck bead pair that could not be pulled apart, but could be touched end by end), the same pattern held.
numbers: Exp 2: 40 preschoolers. All Beads 1/20 (5%) vs Some Beads 9/20 (45%), chi2(1,N=40)=8.53, p<.005. Coder agreement 96% (hypothesis-blind coder used). Overall play variety did not differ, t(40)=0.89, ns.
limits: Same lab, same paradigm, same N per cell. Informative action is rare in the ambiguous cell too: 55% still did not do it. Criterion was conservative (both ends had to be tried).
agent_relevance: Treat as one lab, one paradigm, N=40 per experiment. Supports 'ambiguity triggers a discriminating test' but gives no number for an agent.

source: Moeller, Sodian & Sobel (2022) Developmental trajectories in diagnostic reasoning (Frontiers in Psychology 13:800226)
finding: Closest follow-up to Cook et al. found. It is a conceptual extension with a different paradigm (bricks, controlled-test choice), not a direct replication. Children recognised confounded evidence only partly, and that skill was unrelated to choosing the informative (controlled) test.
numbers: N=57 children aged 3-6. Controlled-test choice on 66% of two-variable trials and 43% of three-variable trials (above chance in some tasks). 70% picked a controlled test at least once in the two-variable task. Just over half recognised the ambiguity of data on at least one trial; about a quarter could say confounded evidence supports no conclusion. Recognition and control-of-variables choice were unrelated.
limits: Not an exact replication. The paper cites Cook et al. as showing spontaneous information seeking and does not re-run it. Choice tasks differ from free play.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: no direct replication found, but a conceptual follow-up supports above-chance informative choice and weakens the claim that children know why. Agent lesson: an explicit ambiguity check and a test chooser may be separate skills.

source: Ruggeri, Lombrozo, Griffiths & Xu (2016) Sources of developmental change in the efficiency of information search (Dev Psych 52:2159), Study 1 (question asking)
finding: Primary numbers for a later child EIG study. Hierarchical 20-questions game. An optimal EIG asker needs 2.85 questions; even adults need more. Children fall short on both question quality and stopping.
numbers: Study 1: 24 second graders (mean 90.5 mo), 23 fifth graders (mean 119.4 mo), adults (error df 67). Questions to solution: 7-year-olds 4.92 (SE .34), 10-year-olds 4.38 (SE .35), adults 3.36 (SE .35); age effect F(2,67)=5.29, p=.007, eta2=.136. Optimal simulation 2.85. Mean question IG: participants 0.83, random 0.50, optimal history-matched 1.06 (F(2,134)=697.97). Adults above optimal count, t(321)=3.143, p=.002.
limits: Lab task with 8 objects and a fixed hierarchy; IG computed against a known hypothesis space. Not a test of whether children compute EIG.
agent_relevance: Human questioners sit between random and optimal even as adults; supports putting EIG in code rather than trusting a free-form question. Closes the Ruggeri 2016 part of gap 5.

source: Ruggeri et al. (2016), stopping rule: unnecessary questions after one hypothesis remained
finding: Many participants kept asking after only one hypothesis remained. Those questions have zero information gain. This is a human over-asking measure.
numbers: Study 1: in at least one trial, 83% of 7-year-olds (n=20), 70% of 10-year-olds (n=16) and 52% of adults (n=12) asked more questions than needed. Study 2 (object selection; 22 second graders, 23 fifth graders, adults): adults 4.11 selections vs optimal 4.17; all participants 5.95 on average; children again continued past the point of one remaining hypothesis. Most unnecessary questions got negative feedback, so reward-seeking does not explain them.
quote: children not only asked questions that were less informative than those of adults
limits: Child stopping rule may reflect low trust in own inference. No cost per question was measured.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: over-asking is an observed human failure and a stop rule (posterior has one hypothesis, or max EIG near zero) is a separate component from question choice.

source: Nelson, Divjak, Gudmundsdottir, Martignon & Meder (2014) Children's sequential information search is sensitive to environmental probabilities (Cognition 130:74)
finding: Only the PubMed abstract was readable (journal text paywalled, no open copy found). Fourth graders judged question usefulness well and adapted to environment statistics; searches were especially efficient in a realistic environment.
numbers: Abstract only: 4th-grade children, yes/no questions, exhaustive search used to find best strategies. Sample size and per-condition figures not obtained.
limits: Primary numbers still unread. Do not cite counts from this paper.
agent_relevance: Gap 5 stays partly open for Nelson 2014: only the qualitative result is confirmed.

source: Pedrozo, Soares & de Oliveira (2026) Do reasoning models ask better questions? (arXiv 2601.17716), win rate and IG
finding: Reasoning mode raises information gain per turn and win rate on a partially observable Guess-My-City game, but only open Qwen3 models of 8B and 30B size were tested, and the effect is largest where the model must build the hypothesis space itself.
numbers: 40 cities x 3 runs = 120 games per model, 30-turn cap. Partially observable (PO): Qwen3-30B Instruct (no thinking) win rate 0.10, IG/turn 0.14, 29.1 turns; Qwen3-30B Thinking win 0.93, IG/turn 0.42, 14.9 turns. Qwen3-8B PO no CoT win 0.08 vs CoT 0.94 (IG/turn 0.17 vs 0.41). Llama-3.1-8B PO win 0.81, IG/turn 0.35. Fully observable: win about 0.77-1.00; IG/turn 0.41-0.78.
limits: Open 8B-30B models only, yes/no questions, one oracle/pruner model (Qwen3-8B), small knowledge graph (max 5.32 bits). No o-series, Claude or Gemini 2.5.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: reasoning raises question quality a lot for small models, so a scaffold gain over a non-reasoning baseline can be inflated; see d08 for how often the reasoning model picks the best question.

source: Pedrozo et al. (2026), decision quality inside reasoning traces
finding: When reasoning models list candidate questions in their thinking and then pick one, they pick the max-IG candidate only a minority of the time.
numbers: Avg Optimal Rate (share of turns choosing the best listed candidate): Qwen3-30B-Thinking FO 0.26, PO 0.25; Qwen3-8B FO 0.36, PO 0.19. Chosen IG vs best listed IG (bits): 30B FO 0.77 vs 1.40; 30B PO 0.43 vs 0.88; 8B FO 0.66 vs 1.11; 8B PO 0.41 vs 0.94. Candidates per turn 5.05-9.74. Candidates parsed from traces with Gemini 2.5 Flash.
limits: Parsing of traces by another LLM; IG computed on a hypothesis space pruned by an LLM agent. Small open models.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: the model generates decent candidates but does not rank them well. This is the step an EIG-in-code selector replaces. Direct evidence that thinking models leave EIG gain on the table (for these sizes).

source: Deng, Li, Li, Zhu, Zhao, Guo & Wang (2026) Uncertainty-aware clarification in LLM agents with information gain (arXiv 2606.03135)
finding: Training a small clarifier with an information-gain reward gives a modest gain in tool-agent success and far fewer clarification turns than general LLMs; an untrained clarifier can hurt.
numbers: Tau-bench-style retail and airline. Averaged over five agent backbones: no clarification 23.6%, Qwen3-8B clarifier 23.0% (-0.6), learned 1.7B clarifier 27.3% (+3.7). Airline +5.4, retail +1.4. DeepSeek-R1 agent: 35.7 -> 40.0 (+4.3). Qwen3-8B as agent with Qwen3-8B clarifier: 15.4 -> 11.9 (-3.5), airline -6.3. Learned clarifier uses 1.3 turns vs 3.9-5.1 for general LLMs; adds about 0.3 total steps.
limits: Success rates are low (15-40%). Reward is a learned belief update toward the ground-truth goal, not computed EIG over sampled hypotheses. Trained, not a scaffold. Preprint.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: a clarifier without an information target can lower success by asking wrong or too many questions; this prices over-asking in tool-agent tasks.

source: Deng et al. (2026), clarification budget sweep
finding: More clarification is not better. Success peaks at a middle budget and then plateaus or falls; extra turns add steps without gain.
numbers: Raising the maximum clarification budget from 0 to a moderate level lifted average success from about 15% to over 21%. Total steps went 24.2 (budget 0) -> 22.1 (budget 2, no success gain) -> 26.5 (budget 6) -> 23.6 (budget 16) -> 25.1 beyond 16 with no success gain. Authors attribute the decline to context pollution and redundant interactions.
limits: Read from text describing a figure; exact success numbers per budget not tabulated. One benchmark.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: a wasted question has a measurable cost (context pollution, extra steps, lower success past a budget). Supports a hard cap plus a value-of-information stop gate.

source: Zhang & Choi (2023) Clarify when necessary (arXiv 2311.09469), when-to-ask gates
finding: Compared four gates for whether to ask: likelihood, Self-Ask, semantic entropy over outputs, and entropy over simulated user intents (user simulation). The best gates reach AUROC only about 0.6 on QA and are near chance on translation.
numbers: AUROC, QA GPT-3: Likelihood .590, Self-Ask .538, Semantic entropy .625, User Sim (entropy over intents) .628. MT GPT-3: .547, .371, .531, .512. LLaMA-2 7B QA: .501-.532. At a 30% clarification budget on QA GPT-3 the semantic-entropy and user-sim gates captured about 49% of the total gain from clarifying everything (random would capture 30%). Some gates gave negative gain for LLaMA-2 7B (e.g. -11% MT likelihood at 30%).
limits: 2023 models (GPT-3, LLaMA-2); entropy from 10 samples is coarse and gave ties; single clarification turn; QA/MT/NLI, not agent tasks.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: entropy over simulated intents is among the best gates but is weak. Treat a gate as a soft signal; do not rely on one number.

source: Zhang, Knox & Choi (2025) Modeling future conversation turns to teach LLMs to ask clarifying questions (ICLR 2025), clarify-or-answer
finding: Training on simulated future-turn outcomes teaches the model when to ask. A prompted ambiguity check (ProCoT) did worst. The trained model avoids clarifying when it could not use the answer.
numbers: Table 4 (Llama2 base): Random gate (44% direct answer) Ans F1 23.4, direct-answer accuracy 55.4, ambiguity accuracy 52.1; Ours (44%) 24.3 / 61.9 / 53.7; Ours with ProCoT gate (35%) F1 15.6, ambiguity acc 49.2; Ours with PPDPP gate (46%) F1 23.9 with about 10 points higher ambiguity accuracy but lower answer F1. Double-turn preference labels give +4-5 F1 over single-turn labels on three base models.
limits: Open-domain QA with 3.7 interpretations on average; trained model, not a scaffold; gain over a random gate is about 1 F1 point.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: the best gate here is trained on expected downstream value, not an ambiguity detector. Mildly supports 'expected gain minus cost' over 'is it ambiguous', but the margin is small.

source: Piriyakulkij, Langenfeld, Le & Ellis (2024) Doing experiments and revising rules (arXiv 2402.06025), Table 1 row mapping
finding: Resolves the critique's open Zendo-row dispute. Table 1 and Table 3 agree once rows are read in order: online fuzzy 5.35, batch hard 6.01, batch refinement hard 6.18, online hard 6.55; Direct LLM (ReAct) 4.60; batch fuzzy about 4.57. The earlier b16 reading (online fuzzy 6.01) is wrong; a26 (online fuzzy 5.35) is right. Row mapping is inferred, not read from clean cells.
numbers: Zendo accuracy out of 8 test scenes: human 5.26; Direct LLM 4.60 (SE .19); online fuzzy 5.35 (SE .09, also in Table 3 InfoGain column); online hard 6.55 (SE .13). Text says strongest model 6.55/8 and fuzzy 5.35/8. R2 with human per-rule accuracy: fuzzy online .57, hard .10, batch .05, ReAct .25.
limits: Table extraction is garbled; mapping inferred from two tables plus text. Zendo accuracy is predictive posterior over test scenes, not task success.
agent_relevance: Gap 8 housekeeping: use 4.60 (ReAct) vs 6.55 (online hard + InfoGain) as the pair. Fuzzy rules fit humans; hard rules score higher.

source: Piriyakulkij et al. (2024), what makes the gain: InfoGain vs LLM-chosen vs random experiments
finding: On Zendo, choosing the experiment by information gain beats letting the LLM choose and beats random choice. A random proposer with 10 candidates matches an LLM proposer, so the selection rule matters more than who writes the candidates.
numbers: Table 3 (online, 5 seeds): Hard rules: LLM-chosen experiment 4.72 (SE .08), Random 5.84 (.19), InfoGain 6.55 (.13). Fuzzy rules: LLM 4.52, Random 5.03, InfoGain 5.35. Table 4: candidate experiments 1/5/10 give about 5.84/6.23/6.55 (random proposer) and 5.73/6.19/6.55 (LLM proposer). ActiveACRE task solving: online hard 0.35 vs batch hard 0.15 and ReAct 0.00.
limits: Toy domains (Zendo scenes, ACRE blickets), 5 seeds, 20 ACRE tasks. LLM-chosen experiment was worse than random, which may reflect prompt design.
agent_relevance: Gaps 1, 7, 8: a baseline ladder (LLM pick < random < InfoGain) at equal candidate count. No strong reasoning model or best-of-N at equal tokens was tested.

source: Choudhury et al. (2026) BED-LLM, Table 1 and Table 3: plain split rule and implicit best-of-M at similar runtime
finding: At about the same wall-clock time as the plain split rule and as 'LLM picks the best of the same candidates', full EIG wins in every model-by-dataset cell of Table 1. This is the nearest thing to an equal-compute comparison found, but it is equal runtime, not equal tokens, and no thinking model was used.
numbers: 20 Questions success %: Animals GPT-4o Split 83, Implicit Max 70, BED-LLM 93; Celebrities GPT-4o 63 / 50 / 86; Things GPT-4o 40 / 42 / 64; Celebrities Mistral-Large 63 / 36 / 91. Runtime Qwen2.5-72B, whole Animals set: BED-LLM 2h30m35s, Implicit Max 2h28m43s, Split 2h46m19s, Entropy 3h10m39s, Data-Estimation 1d17h13m; prompt-only and CoT 26-45 min (row labels garbled). CoT GPT-4o Animals 62.
limits: Yes/no entity tasks with an enumerable hypothesis set. Candidate questions are the same set for IM and BED, so it is not independent best-of-N sampling of whole games. Standard errors 2-5 points.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 partly closed: EIG-in-code beats split rule and LLM-pick at about equal wall-clock. Still open: equal-token comparison with extended thinking and with majority or best-of-N final answers.

source: BED-LLM Appendix F.2 and Fig. 10: Rao-Blackwellised EIG overhead and hypothesis count
finding: The extra conditional-entropy term reuses the same likelihood evaluations, so full EIG costs little more than marginal entropy. In one turn-5 example the ranking of five candidate questions at 10 sampled hypotheses already matched the ranking at 85.
numbers: BED-LLM runtime 2h30m35s vs Entropy 3h10m39s vs Split 2h46m19s (Qwen2.5-72B, Animals). Settings: M=8 candidate questions per turn, at least N=5 hypotheses (convergence figure goes to 85). Ranking at |H|=10 equals ranking at |H|=85. No token counts reported.
limits: One game, one turn, one entity, GPT-4o-mini. Wall-clock depends on hardware and batching. Token overhead still not measured.
agent_relevance: Gap 10 narrowed: cost is dominated by sampling N hypotheses and scoring N x M (hypothesis, question) pairs; ordering is stable at about 10 hypotheses. Exact tokens remain unreported.

source: Kobalczyk et al. (2025) Active task disambiguation, Appendix F cost analysis
finding: States the LLM-call cost per turn. For 20 Questions, EIG needs O(N+M+NM) calls; implicit needs O(1). For code tasks the cost is only O(N+M) because the answers come from running the sampled programs on each question, not from extra LLM calls.
numbers: N = sampled solutions per step, M = candidate questions per step. Implicit-ToT O(M). Authors assume the cost of choosing the query is negligible next to the cost of the oracle answer.
limits: Call counts, not tokens. Authors admit more LLM calls than baselines. Models: GPT-3.5, GPT-4o-mini, Llama-3 8B/70B.
agent_relevance: Gaps 6 and 10: when a test's answer can be computed by running something (code, tool, simulator) the likelihood is deterministic and nearly free; the NM answer calls disappear. This is the cheap case for our agent.

source: BED-LLM Appendix: how hypotheses are generated and filtered (open-set question)
finding: Working recipe for a hypothesis set with no entity list: ask the LLM for N hypotheses in one list with a diversity prompt, filter by answer history, keep earlier survivors, re-ask up to 2-3 times, use a uniform prior. Independent sampling collapses onto a few modes.
numbers: Independent sampling of N=200 hypotheses shows heavy mode collapse (mass on a few figures such as Vincent van Gogh). Settings: joint list generation, temperature 1.3 for 20 Questions (1.0 for preference elicitation), history-compatibility filter threshold 0.2, at least N=5 hypotheses, M=8 candidate questions, most recent Q/A moved to top of context. Mistral-Large Animals: ICL Beliefs (raw, no filter) 53% vs BED-LLM 95%.
limits: Tested on enumerable entities and a preference-elicitation task. No code, proof or research-question task. The filter uses the LLM's own answer probabilities, which Kobalczyk found unreliable as weights.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: best available recipe, untested on open tasks. Sample count for open spaces is unknown; 5-10 worked for entities.

source: Li, Kim & Wang (2025) QuestBench (arXiv 2503.22674), search in code vs LLMs on Logic-Q
finding: A plain breadth-first search in code finds the one needed clarifying question far more often than the strongest LLMs. Gemini 2.5 Pro examples are shown only qualitatively.
numbers: Logic-Q accuracy at predicting the right question: BFS depth 3 = 39.0%, depth 5 = 80.6%, depth 10 = 99.8%; best LLM zero-shot about 50% (o1-preview-class row 49.91%); CoT and 4-shot gave no consistent gains. Planning-Q: best LLM about 40-47%. GSME-Q and GSM-Q: LLMs 90%+ (saturated).
limits: Single-missing-variable logic and planning; table extraction is garbled so exact model-to-row mapping is uncertain. Models tested are 2024-early 2025 (o1-preview, Gemini 2.0 Flash Thinking, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, GPT-4o).
agent_relevance: Gap 2: a reasoning model of that generation did not reliably find the right question, while code search did. Newest models (o3, Claude extended thinking, Gemini 2.5) have no published number.

source: Search outcome for gaps 1, 6, 7, 9 (negative result)
finding: In the reachable sources no paper was found that (a) compares EIG-in-code with best-of-N or majority-of-thinking at equal total tokens, (b) compares Shannon EIG with probability gain or expected error reduction for LLM agents, (c) measures LLM-estimated likelihoods for tool outputs, or (d) tests an incorrect or noisy answerer beyond an LLM-to-LLM mismatch.
numbers: Search status: WebSearch budget ran out after 4 queries, then refilled for 1 query (returned BED-LLM, Mazzaccara, UoT only); arXiv API returned HTTP 429 or empty; Semantic Scholar 429; OpenAlex budget exhausted. Papers newly read: Pedrozo 2026, Deng 2026, Zhang and Knox 2025, Moeller 2022, Ruggeri 2016. Re-read for new facts: BED-LLM, Kobalczyk, Piriyakulkij, QuestBench, Zhang and Choi.
limits: Absence of evidence under a rate-limited search, not proof nothing exists. A later pass with working search should retry gaps 1, 6, 7, 9 first.
agent_relevance: Treat gaps 1, 6, 7, 9 as open. Design them as our own bench arms: EIG-code vs best-of-N vs split at equal tokens; probability gain vs Shannon; noisy answerer at 10/20/30% flip rate.
